items.situation: Describe the annual review as a process. Say it.
tips: Present simple passive -- the process, not the person.

items.situation: State the California rule about job ads. Say it.
tips: The range must be posted in the ad.

items.situation: Finance finished updating the Texas bands this week. Say it.
tips: The Texas bands have been updated.
Present perfect passive -- recent, and the result matters now.

items.situation: An outside firm checked the bands because you asked. Say it.
tips: We had the bands audited by an outside firm.
Have something done -- somebody else did it for you.

items.situation: You chose not to match an offer. Tell the CEO.
tips: I decided not to match the offer.
Active voice: a decision has a name attached to it.

items.situation: Explain the Austin and Sacramento gap in one sentence.
tips: The difference is explained by cost of living, and nothing else.

listenings.text: Every new client shows me their base salaries first, and I understand why. It is the number on the offer letter. But it is not what people compare once they are inside. In the US, the health plan can be worth twenty or thirty percent of the salary, and the employer match on retirement is the first thing an experienced engineer asks about. So when I am asked, are we paying enough, my first answer is always another question: enough of what? The second thing I tell clients is about transparency. In California, Washington and a growing list of places, the range has to be published. That means your pay bands are not a private document any more. They are a public promise. If you cannot explain a gap in one sentence, you should assume it will be explained for you, and not kindly.

Two years ago one of our best engineers came to me with an offer from a competitor. Fifteen percent more. We matched it within a day, and I was proud of how fast we moved. Eight months later he left anyway, and this time he did not come to me first. When I looked back, the money had never been the real problem. He had been asking for a different role for a year, and the request had been parked in every review. The counteroffer told him we would pay to keep him, but not that we would change anything. What I do now is simple. When somebody brings me an offer, I ask what they would need to stay if the money were the same. Sometimes the answer is money. More often than not, it is something that should have been fixed a year earlier.
